items.title: Karl-Anthony Towns 'Very Disappointed' By Knicks' Decision To Pause Extension Talks
items.summary: Karl-Anthony Towns said Sunday he was caught off guard by the New York Knicks' decision to delay contract extension talks until later in the season. The team announced late last week that it would not negotiate with eligible players until then. "It was news to me," said Towns. "Very disappointed, to say the least. Let's state the obvious: It's a business, but there is business on the court for us to handle." Towns is one of four Knicks eligible for extensions, along with Josh Hart, Miles McBride and Tyler Kolek. Towns has been the most outspoken of the group about his frustration. The Knicks' offer to Towns has centered on a deal worth close to $200 million in total, league sources said. Towns is eligible to sign for up to a four-year, $276 million extension. The Knicks face tight financial constraints. Owner James Dolan has instructed the front office not to cross the second apron, which has complicated negotiations following the team's NBA championship. The timeline now hinges on Towns' $61 million player option for next season. He must decline it by Oct. 19 to negotiate with the Knicks during the season. If he does not, New York cannot legally discuss an extension with Towns or his representatives until after the season. Towns would then be officially entering the final year of his contract.

items.title: Josh Hart 'Not Too Stressed' About Knicks Stopping Extension Talks
items.summary: New York Knicks wing Josh Hart was asked about the team tabling extension talks for eligible players, such as himself. Hart didn't seem as worried about the situation as teammates Karl-Anthony Towns and Miles McBride seem to be. "Everything is going to work out. I'm not really too stressed over it," Hart said. "I'm not putting too much into it. We have expectations, so it's good we are able to focus on the season." Hart has two years left on his contract. This season, the veteran wing is owed $20.9 million. Next season, the Knicks hold a $22.4 million team option for Hart. In order for Hart to extend after October 19, New York would need to decline that team option first. As things play out, Hart was honest that their next deals would occasionally be on the minds of the extension-eligible players. "There will be days where we don't think about it," Hart said. "There will be days where it's top of the mind. We're humans."

items.title: NBA Pushes Back On Claims Second Apron Hurts Middle-Class Players
items.summary: The NBA issued a statement Friday disputing claims that the second apron had adverse effects upon the league's middle-class players. The league said salaries have grown for players at every pay level since the rule took effect. "Recent reports asserted that the second apron is hurting 'lower' and 'middle' class players," said the NBA in a post on X. "That's untrue. Since the implementation of the second apron, the number of players on team rosters has remained the same and annual salaries have increased by nearly $1.3 billion resulting in pay increases of approximately 30% for all classes of players." The statement came a day after comments from veteran guard Bruce Brown. Brown was asked after Thursday's preseason game between the New York Knicks and Washington Wizards whether players were frustrated by the second apron. "I'm sure there is," said Brown. "The new CBA is good for max guys, new free agents and rookie extension guys. The middle guys, it kind of sucks for us. There's not a lot of people getting that full midlevel." Brown played all 82 games for the Denver Nuggets last season but did not land a guaranteed contract this summer. Brown signed a non-guaranteed training camp deal with the Knicks and is competing for the defending champions' final roster spot. The second apron was introduced as part of the 2023 collective bargaining agreement. Teams above the threshold, set at $209 million this season, lose access to most trades and free-agent signings and can see future draft picks pushed to the end of the first round. No team enters the 2026-27 season above the second apron. Knicks owner James Dolan said in June that his team could not cross the threshold. However, more teams have moved into the luxury tax since 2023. That threshold, which carries lighter penalties, sits just over $200 million.
